title: Reading Input
summary: Read everything sent to your program on stdin, split it into lines and numbers, and print results from it.
intro: Until now every program had its data written in the code. Real programs read data from outside. Here you read everything sent to standard input (stdin), split it into lines and numbers, and print results from it.

steps.title: Reading all of stdin
steps.body:
`require` loads a module. `require("fs")` gives you Node's built-in file system module, and its `readFileSync` reads a whole file at once. File descriptor `0` is stdin, and `"utf8"` asks for a string instead of raw bytes.

```javascript
const input = require("fs").readFileSync(0, "utf8");
```

Read stdin once, at the top of the program. Whatever was sent arrives as one string, usually ending in a newline. `trim()` removes that newline and any spaces at either end.

Input is always text, even when it looks like a number. Convert it with `Number()` before doing math, or `+` will join strings instead of adding.

```stdin
21
```

```javascript harness
const input = require("fs").readFileSync(0, "utf8");
{{code}}
console.log(n, typeof n);
```

```javascript
const n = Number(input.trim()); // "21\n" becomes 21
```

Print only the results. Nobody is typing at a keyboard, so a prompt such as `Enter a number:` would just become wrong output.

**The gotcha:** `%` keeps the sign of the left side, so `-3 % 2` is `-1`, not `1`. Test parity with `n % 2 === 0`, which works for negative numbers too.

example.title: Double a number
example.prompt: Read one integer from stdin, then print it doubled and whether it is even or odd.
example.explanation: `readFileSync(0, "utf8")` returns `"21\n"`. `trim()` drops the newline and `Number()` turns `"21"` into `21`, so `n * 2` is real math. `21 % 2` is `1`, so the even check fails and the else branch prints `21 is odd`.

practice.title: Square a number
practice.prompt:
Read one integer from stdin and print its square and whether it is even or odd.

1. Read all of stdin and convert it to a number `n` with `trim()` and `Number()`.
2. Print `<n> squared is <square>`.
3. Print `<n> is even` or `<n> is odd`. Negative numbers must work too.
4. Print nothing else, no prompts.

Input:

```text
7
```

Expected output:

```text
7 squared is 49
7 is odd
```
hints: Trim the input, then convert it with `Number()`, just like the example.
Check `n % 2 === 0` for even. Comparing with `1` fails for `-3`, because `-3 % 2` is `-1`.

steps.title: Reading lines

example.title: Years until 100
example.prompt: Read a name and an age on two lines, then print how many lines were read and how many years remain until 100.
example.output:
Read 2 lines
Ada is 36, 64 years until 100
example.explanation: `input.trim()` removes the final newline, so `split("\n")` gives exactly `["Ada", "36"]`. Destructuring names the two lines. `ageText` is the string `"36"`, and `Number()` turns it into `36` so `100 - age` is `64`.

practice.title: Order line
practice.prompt:
Read an item name, a price, and a quantity on three lines and print the order total.

1. Split the input into lines and destructure them into `item`, `priceText`, and `quantityText`.
2. Convert the price and quantity with `Number()`.
3. Print `<quantity> x <item> = $<total>`, with the total (price times quantity) formatted to 2 decimal places.

Input:

```text
Blue Pen
1.50
3
```

Expected output:

```text
3 x Blue Pen = $4.50
```
hints: Split the trimmed input on `"\n"` and destructure three names from the result, like the example does with two.
`total.toFixed(2)` gives two decimals. Write `$${...}` to print a dollar sign before the value.

steps.title: Counts and numbers on a line
steps.body:
Many inputs start with a count: the first line says how many lines follow. With the lines in `lines = input.trim().split("\n")`, read the count from `lines[0]`, then take the rest with `slice`. `lines.slice(1)` gives every line after the first, and `slice(1, n + 1)` keeps exactly `n` of them.

```stdin
2
9  4
1 2 3
```

```javascript harness
const input = require("fs").readFileSync(0, "utf8");
const lines = input.trim().split("\n");
{{code}}
console.log(n, rows);
```

```javascript
const n = Number(lines[0]);
const rows = lines.slice(1, n + 1); // the n lines after the count
```

To turn a line of numbers into an array, trim it, split on `/\s+/` (one or more whitespace characters: spaces, tabs, or newlines), and map each piece through `Number`.

```javascript harness
const line = "9  4";
{{code}}
console.log(nums);
```

```javascript
const nums = line.trim().split(/\s+/).map(Number); // "9  4" becomes [9, 4]
```

Do not use `split(" ")`: a doubled space makes an empty token, and `Number("")` is `0`, a silent wrong value.

Always write `.map(Number)`, never `.map(parseInt)`. `map` calls its callback with the value *and* the index, and `parseInt` reads its second argument as the radix (number base). So `["10", "10", "10"].map(parseInt)` gives `[10, NaN, 2]`: base 0 means default, base 1 is invalid, and `"10"` in base 2 is 2.

When line breaks do not matter, read every token at once. Because `\s` also matches newlines, `"3\n4 5\n6"` becomes `[3, 4, 5, 6]`.

```stdin
3
4 5
6
```

```javascript harness
const input = require("fs").readFileSync(0, "utf8");
{{code}}
console.log(tokens);
```

```javascript
const tokens = input.trim().split(/\s+/).map(Number);
```

example.title: Line sums
example.prompt: Read a count n, then n lines of numbers, and print each line's sum and max followed by the grand total.
example.output:
Line 1: sum 12, max 8
Line 2: sum 13, max 9
Line 3: sum 24, max 10
Total: 49
example.explanation: `lines[0]` is the count. `lines.slice(1, n + 1)` keeps the next three lines, and `entries()` gives each one with its index. `split(/\s+/)` treats the doubled space in `9  4` as one gap, so `map(Number)` gives `[9, 4]` instead of `[9, 0, 4]`. `reduce` adds each line, `Math.max(...nums)` finds its largest value, and `total` collects every sum.

practice.title: Student averages
practice.prompt:
Read a count n and then n lines of test scores, one student per line, and report each student's average.

1. Read `n` from the first line.
2. For each of the next `n` lines, turn the scores into an array of numbers. A line can hold any number of scores.
3. Print `Student <number>: <average>` with the average to 2 decimal places, numbering students from 1 in input order.
4. Finally print `Above 80: <count>`, the number of students whose average is strictly greater than 80.

Input:

```text
3
90 85 77
60 70 80
100 95
```

Expected output:

```text
Student 1: 84.00
Student 2: 70.00
Student 3: 97.50
Above 80: 2
```
hints: Loop over `lines.slice(1, n + 1).entries()` to get each line with its index.
`line.trim().split(/\s+/).map(Number)` gives the scores. Divide their sum by `scores.length`.
An average of exactly 80 does not count, so test `average > 80`.

recap:
- `require("fs").readFileSync(0, "utf8")` reads all of stdin as one string. Read it once, at the top.
- `trim()` removes the trailing newline. Input is always text, so convert with `Number()`.
- Print only results, never prompts.
- `input.trim().split("\n")` gives the lines, and `const [a, b] = lines` names them.
- A count on the first line tells you how many lines follow. `lines.slice(1)` gives the rest.
- `line.trim().split(/\s+/).map(Number)` turns a line of numbers into an array. Never `split(" ")`, never `.map(parseInt)`.
- `input.trim().split(/\s+/)` reads every token at once when line breaks do not matter.
